newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt faces parliament wrath over cuts.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt faces parliament wrath over cuts.

text.p: Russia's new reformist government faces a first big clash with the communist-dominated parliament on Wednesday when it presents its accounts for the first quarter and a bill demanding drastic spending cuts.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who saw his cabinet reshuffled and rejuvenated by President Boris Yeltsin two months ago, will seek to explain to the largely hostile State Duma lower house why millions of pensioners and state employees are owed benefits and wages going back months.

His first deputy, Anatoly Chubais, a free-marketeer who is a particular hate figure for the communists, is expected to present a bill calling for spending cuts of 108 trillion roubles ($19 billion), or about 20 percent of the 1997 budget.
The government justifies the measure on the grounds that it gathered little more than half the tax revenue it had budgeted for in the first three months of the year.
The communists, the biggest single bloc in the Duma, have said the cuts are unacceptable and have called for compromise.
Chubais launched a pre-emptive strike on Tuesday, chiding the Duma for dodging its responsibilities and failing to propose its own solutions to the budget crisis.
"The question is, do the deputies of the State Duma have the courage to formulate decisions on what everyone considers essential?" he told Russian television stations.
"We cannot have in Russia's state finances a whole year where the budget is only half met. It opens fantastic opportunities for manipulation," he added.

The parliamentary leader of the Our Home is Russia government party told NTV television the Duma could, as it did last year, avoid the responsibility of voting a budget package by giving ministers a simple order to put the economy right.
Echoing earlier comments from Chernomyrdin, Chubais insisted the government was open to suggestions and ready to do a deal.
"Our positions are not cast in stone," Chubais said.
"Quite the reverse, we're ready to listen to any arguments and reach a compromise."

On past experience, some form of bargain seems likely, although all sides will probably want to avoid a repeat of the original 1997 finance act, which ended up pleasing virtually no one and which Yeltsin immediately condemned as "a bad budget".

The Duma has little power to overrule government policy. Any vote of no confidence could end up with the president dissolving the chamber, a prospect many communist deputies, elected on a wave of anti-Yeltsin feeling 18 months ago, do not relish.
Chernomyrdin has already indicated that the government is looking for extra sources of revenue that might allow it to soften the effects of some of the cuts.
The lack of revenue plan to accompany the cuts has been a key complaint of the opposition, on all sides of the chamber.

Liberal Yabloko party leader Grigory Yavlinsky has been seeking support for a -- largely symbolic -- no-confidence motion, primarily based on the chaotic state of the nation's finances and the government's failure to raise more revenue.

The Duma is due to vote on the cuts plan, known as the sequestration bill, on Friday. On Tuesday, its economics committee recommended delaying the vote, however, until the government made some proposals on finding new income.
Longer term, raising income through reforming the complex and much abused tax system is a priority for the government's young reformers. But that is an issue for the 1998 budget.
In the meantime, it is likely to be a case of muddling through. As Chubais put it: "Let's see how things work out."
